The Atlantic mudskipper Periophthalmus barbarus is an amphibious goby that inhabits intertidal mudflats and mangrove forests along the West African coast. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched prolarvae emerge from demersal eggs weighing approximately 0.00021 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00021 grams], a mass derived from eggs measuring about 1.1 millimeters in length and 0.6 millimeters in width. At a consistent water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], these yolk-sac larvae undergo eclosion roughly 7.5 days [ab = roughly 7.5 days] after fertilization, transitioning quickly from lecithotrophic dependence to active feeding on microcrustaceans. This brief embryonic period is typical for small-bodied gobiids and reflects the species adaptation to warm, variable thermal regimes in their intertidal nursery habitats, where rapid development is advantageous before tidal exposure events.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a body length of approximately 9.6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 9.6 centimeters], at which point individuals weigh around 7.2 grams [Wwp = around 7.2 grams] based on length-mass regressions derived from captured specimens. This transition to the sub-adult stage involves gonadal recrudescence and the onset of gametogenesis, marking puberty as a key life history event. The size at maturation is relatively modest compared to other members of the family Oxudercidae, likely reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a semiterrestrial lifestyle where foraging time on land must be balanced against the risk of desiccation and predation. Once maturity is attained, individuals direct resources toward reproductive effort, with gravid females producing multiple clutches during the breeding season.

At a stable thermal regime of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], reproductively active females achieve a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 65.6 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 65.6 eggs per day] averaged over the year. This high fecundity is supported by field observations of nest-guarding adults that deposit their clutch in burrows excavated in the soft mud, providing a humid microhabitat that protects the developing embryos from extreme thermal fluctuations. The rate at which eggs are produced reflects the species iteroparous strategy, with females capable of repeated spawning events throughout the extended breeding season. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this level of reproductive investment is among the highest recorded for amphibious gobies, likely an adaptation to high juvenile mortality rates in the variable intertidal environment.

Adult males of Periophthalmus barbarus attain a maximum total length of 14.7 centimeters [Li = 14.7 centimeters], corresponding to an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 25 grams [Wwi = approximately 25 grams] calculated from length-weight relationships. This maximum body size is achieved through a growth trajectory that decelerates markedly after the pubertal transition, with older individuals investing progressively more energy into reproductive activities rather than somatic growth. Under controlled laboratory conditions at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the oldest documented individuals have reached a maximum lifespan of 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days], equivalent to roughly five years, though wild populations likely experience higher mortality rates from avian predation and habitat disturbance.

The species amphibious nature imposes distinct physiological demands that shape its life history strategy, particularly regarding the trade-off between growth and reproduction. The yolk-dependent prolarvae that hatch at 7.5 days [ab = 7.5 days] post-fertilization at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] must rapidly develop the capacity for aerial respiration as they transition from aquatic to semi-terrestrial habitats. The maximum recorded longevity of five years [am = five years] observed under stable captive conditions at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] is consistent with that of other small-bodied gobiids, though the species amphibious behavior may expose it to increased metabolic costs associated with maintaining osmoregulatory balance across the air-water interface. These ecological constraints collectively shape a life history characterized by rapid early development, early maturity, and high fecundity.
